item.title: The Middle East War Has Wiped 2.8 Billion Barrels Off Global Oil Supply
item.description: The war in the Middle East has caused global oil supply losses of a total of 2.8 billion barrels plus 60 billion cubic meters of natural gas, the International Energy Agency estimated in its latest World Energy Outlook, released today. This disruption is going to affect oil demand, the IEA predicted, but only if governments around the world stay the course with accelerated electrification to reduce consumption of hydrocarbons. item.title: EU Delays Methane Rules by Two Years Amid Energy Supply Fears
item.description: The European Parliament and EU member states agreed today to delay the so-called methane regulation by two years under pressure from the top oil and gas supplier, the United States, and the continued disruption of normal supply resulting from the war in the Middle East. item.title: Oil Prices Steady as Hormuz Tanker Threats Offset Supply Glut Fears
item.description: Crude oil prices steadied today after a decline earlier this week, as the perception of a return to oversupply and continued attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz basically canceled each other out. At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $92.01 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $83.00 per barrel, as forecasters warn of a glut even though tanker tracking data shows flows out of the Persian Gulf are still below pre-war levels, despite the significant improvement from the early months of the war. item.title: Inside the Army’s 75 Year Plan to Escape China’s Rare Earth Dominance
item.description: Over the past several years, the U.S. government has committed billions of dollars to solving the rare earth supply problem. MP Materials received more than $1 billion in combined financing. USA Rare Earth secured a $1.6 billion government financing package. The Department of Defense and Department of Energy have funded pilot programs, feasibility studies, and demonstration projects across the sector. item.title: Permian Growth Turns Moderate Despite War
item.description: Crude oil production in the most prolific basin in the United States has remained moderate despite the war premium that pushed prices to over $100 a barrel. For some, however, the very fact of production growth in the Permian is a surprise. The Permian has been the engine driving U.S. crude oil output growth for over a decade. Annual growth in the past consistently exceeded 1 million barrels--until 2020, when pandemic lockdowns killed demand and plunged U.S. crude into negative territory briefly. item.title: Google Signs Landmark Superhot Geothermal Deal
item.description: The AI boom and the hyperscalers’ need for round-the-clock clean energy for their data centers meet the next-generation geothermal energy technologies developed by a number of start-ups. In a world first, Google this week signed an agreement with Quaise Energy to use power from the superhot rocks in the Newberry Volcano in Oregon for its existing data center operations in The Dalles. item.title: Equinor Hack Adds to Wave of Cyberattacks on Energy Companies
item.description: Equinor, the largest supplier of pipeline gas to Europe, is fighting an ongoing cyberattack on its IT systems while the Hormuz crisis keeps European gas prices nearly triple last year’s level. The FBI warned last week that state-aligned hackers and criminals are using an AI-powered tool to break into corporate networks in under three hours. item.title: China Burns Less Oil and Coal as the Iran War Reshapes Its Energy Mix
item.description: The war in Iran is causing an enduring upset in global oil and gas markets with long-ranging consequences for the economy, the energy sector, and the climate. For many countries, this has resulted in skyrocketing energy prices and a rapid shift toward renewable energies in order to fill the import gap. For China, the global leader in clean energy supply chains by a massive margin, this has resulted in a windfall – and a drop in greenhouse gas emissions. item.description: The saga of financially distressed Thames Water may have reached a new low. item.title: Iraq's Border Shutdown With Iran Threatens a Much Bigger Economic Crisis
item.description: Iraq’s closure of the Al-Sheeb crossing with Iran is less an economic rupture than a test of whether Baghdad can secure its borders without damaging its economy. The immediate costs are concentrated in Maysan Province and are manageable, at least for now. A wider, prolonged shutdown would be different: it would disrupt trade, raise costs for Iraqi businesses and consumers, and complicate Baghdad’s effort to establish Iraq as a regional transportation and logistics hub. item.description: QazaqGaz, Kazakhstan’s vertically integrated national gas company, has signed a contract with a Chinese consortium to build a gas processing plant with an annual capacity of 2.5 billion cubic meters (bcm) pumped from the Kashagan field. item.title: Copper Heads for Longest Weekly Losing Streak in Two Years
item.description: Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) beat Wall Street’s revenue forecast by about $6.7 billion on Tuesday night, and copper fell for a fifth straight session on Wednesday. item.title: Mozambique Approves Exxon’s Redesigned $30 Billion Rovuma LNG Plan
item.description: Mozambique’s Council of Ministers on Tuesday approved ExxonMobil’s (NYSE:XOM) amended development plan for the Rovuma LNG project, clearing a regulatory hurdle before a final investment decision (FID) the company expects by the end of the year. item.title: Democrats Could Slow Venezuela’s Push Toward 3 Million Bpd
item.description: The Democratic Party’s sweep of the US midterm elections is unlikely to derail Venezuela’s near-term oil recovery, but greater congressional scrutiny could slow the next wave of investment.
